segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Once, while the crowd was pressing in on him and listening to the word of God, he was standing beside Lake Gennesaret,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he saw two boats lying at the edge of the lake; the fishermen had gotten out of them and were washing their nets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He got into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowds from the boat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Master, we worked hard all through the night and caught nothing. But at your word I will let down the nets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had done this, they enclosed a great number of fish, and their nets were beginning to tear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they signaled to their associates in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Simon Peter saw it, he fell at the knees of Jesus and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For amazement had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish they had taken,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Then Jesus said to Simon,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they had brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in one of the towns, there was a man covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am willing. Be made clean.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately the leprosy left him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he ordered him to tell no one:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Instead, go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing as Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the news about him spread all the more, and large crowds were gathering to hear him and to be healed of their illnesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he would withdraw to deserted places and pray.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One day, while he was teaching, there were Pharisees and teachers of the Law sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then some men came carrying a paralyzed man on a bed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down through the tiles, stretcher and all, into the middle in front of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw their faith, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who is this man who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, perceiving their reasoning, answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you reasoning in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I tell you, get up, pick up your stretcher, and go to your house.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he stood up in front of them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went off to his house, glorifying God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Astonishment seized them all, and they glorified God; they were filled with fear and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have seen extraordinary things today.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And leaving everything behind, he got up and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Levi gave a great banquet for him in his house, and there was a large crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining at table with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees and their scribes were grumbling to his disciples, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Those who are healthy have no need of a doctor, but those who are sick do.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to turning back.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John’s disciples fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You cannot make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them, can you?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also told them a parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “No one tears a patch from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new garment, and the patch from the new will not match the old.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins; it will be spilled, and the skins will be ruined.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But new wine must be put into new wineskins.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one who has drunk old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

notes.note: This is the body of water that Matthew and Mark call the Sea of Galilee. Luke consistently uses the ordinary Greek word for a lake, which is the more exact term for an inland body of fresh water. Gennesaret is the name of the fertile plain on its northwestern shore.

This form of address occurs only in Luke in the New Testament and is always spoken to Jesus. In ordinary Greek it named someone in charge, such as a supervisor or overseer. Luke uses it where the other Gospels often have “Teacher” or “Rabbi.” It is a different word from “Lord” in verse 8.

Most translations have “catching men” or “fishing for people,” echoing the “fishers” saying in Matthew and Mark. Luke’s verb is not a fishing term; it means to capture alive, and in the Septuagint it is used of sparing captives in war. The rendering keeps that sense: fish are caught to die, but these people are to be taken alive. Its only other New Testament use is 2 Timothy 2:26.

The Greek word, as in the Greek version of Leviticus 13–14, covers a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean and excluded them from ordinary community life. It is not limited to, and may not include, what is now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease). This is why the man asks to be made “clean” and not simply healed.

Leviticus 14 requires a person recovered from such a skin disease to be examined by a priest and to bring offerings before returning to normal life. “Them” may be the priests or the people in general, who would then have official evidence of the cure. The Greek could also mean “as a testimony against them,” though most interpreters take it in the neutral sense.

notes.phrase: the power of the Lord was with him to heal
notes.traditional: the power of the Lord was present to heal them
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read “him,” making Jesus the one who heals. Many later manuscripts read “them,” giving “the power of the Lord was present to heal them,” the reading behind the King James Version. “The Lord” here refers to God, whose power is at work in Jesus.

These were local collectors of tolls and customs duties on goods, working for contractors who had bought the right to collect. They were widely regarded as dishonest and as collaborators with the ruling powers, which is why they are paired with “sinners” in verse 30. The “tax booth” was a toll station.

The traditional rendering is “repentance,” and most translations keep it as an established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word here carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, so it is rendered “turning back.”

The Greek is literally “sons of the bridal chamber,” a Semitic turn of phrase for those who belong to the wedding party, whether the groom’s attendants or the guests more broadly. A wedding was a time of feasting, at which fasting would be out of place.

Wine was stored in sewn animal skins. Newly pressed wine continues to ferment and give off gas; a new skin stretches with it, but an old skin that has already stretched and hardened splits. Greek uses two near-synonyms for “new” in these verses, one for the wine and another for the garment and the skins; both are rendered “new” here.

Many manuscripts read “better” where the earliest have “good”; the comparative looks like a scribal sharpening. A few witnesses, including Codex Bezae, omit the whole verse, which has no parallel in Matthew or Mark. The word for “good” here can also mean pleasant or mellow.

candidates.reason: The traditional word suggests Hansen’s disease, while the Greek covers a range of defiling skin conditions; versions vary between “leprosy” and “skin disease,” and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels.
Recurs throughout the Synoptics; “tax collector,” “toll collector,” and “publican” are all in use, and the word should not vary between chapters.
Very frequent in the Gospels and Acts; “scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, while alternatives like “teacher of the law” or “legal expert” collide with νομοδιδάσκαλος and νομικός.
A distinctively Lukan address to Jesus that needs to stay distinct from κύριος, διδάσκαλος, and δεσπότης across Luke’s chapters.

Used across the Gospels both as a moral self-description and as a social label for a class of people (“tax collectors and sinners”); one decision is needed on whether the English stays “sinner” in both uses.
